claim: Midbrain dopaminergic (mDA) neurons migrate to form the laterally-located substantia nigra pars compacta (SN) and medially-located ventral tegmental area (VTA).
source: Midbrain dopaminergic (mDA) neurons migrate to form the laterally-located substantia nigra pars compacta (SN) and medially-located ventral tegmental area (VTA), but little is known about the underlying cellular and molecular processes.
evidence: This is a statement of established anatomical knowledge about mDA neuron migration patterns.

claim: Little is known about the cellular and molecular processes underlying mDA neuron migration.
source: Midbrain dopaminergic (mDA) neurons migrate to form the laterally-located substantia nigra pars compacta (SN) and medially-located ventral tegmental area (VTA), but little is known about the underlying cellular and molecular processes.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field, indicating a gap in understanding.

claim: SN-mDA neurons exhibit two distinct migration modes: slow migration and fast, laterally-directed migration.
source: Here we visualize the dynamic cell morphologies of tangentially migrating SN-mDA neurons in 3D and identify two distinct migration modes. Slow migration is the default mode in SN-mDA neurons, while fast, laterally-directed migration occurs infrequently and is strongly associated with bipolar cell morphology.
evidence: This claim is supported by the time-lapse imaging data and analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Slow migration is the default mode in SN-mDA neurons.
source: Slow migration is the default mode in SN-mDA neurons, while fast, laterally-directed migration occurs infrequently and is strongly associated with bipolar cell morphology.
evidence: This is supported by the frequency analysis of migration speeds in the manuscript.

claim: Fast, laterally-directed migration occurs infrequently in SN-mDA neurons.
source: Slow migration is the default mode in SN-mDA neurons, while fast, laterally-directed migration occurs infrequently and is strongly associated with bipolar cell morphology.
evidence: This is supported by the frequency analysis of migration speeds in the manuscript.

claim: Fast, laterally-directed migration is strongly associated with bipolar cell morphology.
source: Slow migration is the default mode in SN-mDA neurons, while fast, laterally-directed migration occurs infrequently and is strongly associated with bipolar cell morphology.
evidence: This is supported by the morphological analysis of migrating neurons at different speeds.

claim: Tangential migration of SN-mDA neurons is altered in absence of Reelin signaling.
source: Tangential migration of SN-mDA neurons is altered in absence of Reelin signaling, but it is unclear whether Reelin acts directly on migrating SN-mDA neurons and how it affects their cell morphology and migratory behavior.
evidence: This is supported by previous studies and the current manuscript's data on Dab1 mutants.

claim: It is unclear whether Reelin acts directly on migrating SN-mDA neurons.
source: Tangential migration of SN-mDA neurons is altered in absence of Reelin signaling, but it is unclear whether Reelin acts directly on migrating SN-mDA neurons and how it affects their cell morphology and migratory behavior.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in knowledge that the manuscript aims to address.

claim: Reelin signaling acts directly on mDA neurons to regulate their tangential migration.
source: By specifically inactivating Reelin signaling in mDA neurons we demonstrate its direct role in SN-mDA tangential migration.
evidence: This is demonstrated through conditional knockout experiments (Dab1 CKO) presented in the manuscript.

claim: Reelin promotes laterally-biased movements in mDA neurons during their slow migration mode.
source: Reelin promotes laterally-biased movements in mDA neurons during their slow migration mode, stabilizes leading process morphology and increases the probability of fast, laterally-directed migration.
evidence: This is supported by trajectory analysis comparing control and Dab1-/- neurons.

claim: Reelin stabilizes leading process morphology in mDA neurons.
source: Reelin promotes laterally-biased movements in mDA neurons during their slow migration mode, stabilizes leading process morphology and increases the probability of fast, laterally-directed migration.
evidence: This is supported by morphological analysis showing increased branch transitions in Dab1-/- neurons.

claim: Reelin increases the probability of fast, laterally-directed migration in mDA neurons.
source: Reelin promotes laterally-biased movements in mDA neurons during their slow migration mode, stabilizes leading process morphology and increases the probability of fast, laterally-directed migration.
evidence: This is supported by the analysis of maximum speed distributions in control vs. Dab1-/- neurons.

claim: Dysfunction in the dopaminergic system is associated with schizophrenia, addiction and depression.
source: Dysfunction in the dopaminergic system is associated with schizophrenia, addiction and depression, and degeneration of mDA neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta (SN) results in the motor symptoms of Parkinson's disease (Grace and Bunney, 1980; Volkow and Morales, 2015; Przedborski, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: SN-mDA neurons project predominantly to the dorsal striatum and modulate voluntary movement.
source: SN-mDA neurons project predominantly to the dorsal striatum and modulate voluntary movement (Weisenhorn et al., 2016), while VTA-mDA neurons project to various forebrain targets, including the prefrontal cortex, nucleus accumbens and basolateral amygdala, and are important for the regulation of cognitive function and reward behavior (Morales and Margolis, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: mDA neuron differentiation starts at embryonic day (E) 10.5 in the mouse.

evidence: This is a statement of established developmental timing.

source: In Dab1 CKO mice, TH+, SOX6+ and TH+, Lmo3+ mDA neurons were more medially located than in controls and were partially intermingled with TH+, OTX2+ mDA neurons at the border between SN and lateral VTA (Figure 3E,G,I).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The inactivation of Reelin signaling in mDA neurons results in an ectopic medial location of SN-mDA neurons and a partial mixing of the two populations at what would constitute the SN-lateral VTA border in control brains.
source: Hence, the inactivation of Reelin signaling in mDA neurons results in an ectopic medial location of SN-mDA neurons and a partial mixing of the two populations at what would constitute the SN-lateral VTA border in control brains.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the marker expression analysis.

claim: In both control and Dab1-/- embryonic brains at E13.5, TH+ fibers extended from the midbrain to the forebrain.
source: In both control and Dab1-/- embryonic brains, TH+ fibers extended from the midbrain to the forebrain (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-D).
evidence: This is supported by whole-mount immunostaining data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: At P30, the density of TH+ fibers was similar in the striatum of control and Dab1-/- brains.
source: At P30, the density of TH+ fibers was similar in the striatum of control and Dab1-/- brains (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E-G, three rostrocaudal levels).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining and quantification data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Loss of Reelin signaling and the consequent changes in the anatomical organization of mDA neuronal cell bodies do not seem to affect general axon pathfinding processes in mDA neurons.
source: Hence, loss of Reelin signaling and the consequent changes in the anatomical organization of mDA neuronal cell bodies do not seem to affect general axon pathfinding processes in mDA neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the analysis of axonal projections.

claim: More than two-thirds of YFP-labeled neurons are TH+ in the imaged regions at E13.5 in the genetic fate mapping system used.
source: With this system, SN-mDA neurons are preferentially labeled and more than two-thirds of YFP-labeled neurons are TH+ in the imaged regions at E13.5, and almost 90% are TH+ at E14.5 (Blaess et al., 2011; Bodea et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work from the authors' laboratory.

claim: Almost 90% of YFP-labeled neurons are TH+ in the imaged regions at E14.5 in the genetic fate mapping system used.
source: With this system, SN-mDA neurons are preferentially labeled and more than two-thirds of YFP-labeled neurons are TH+ in the imaged regions at E13.5, and almost 90% are TH+ at E14.5 (Blaess et al., 2011; Bodea et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work from the authors' laboratory.

claim: The behavior of cells in different control slices and in different Dab1-/- slices was comparable.
source: Plotting average speed distributions of cells from each slice, showed that the behavior of cells in different control slices and in different Dab1-/- slices was comparable (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Individual cells' soma speeds varied considerably over time.
source: However, individual cells' soma speeds varied considerably over time, and the maximum observed soma speed (henceforth max-speed) of a cell could be several times higher than its average speed (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by speed profile analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: The maximum observed soma speed (max-speed) of a cell could be several times higher than its average speed.
source: However, individual cells' soma speeds varied considerably over time, and the maximum observed soma speed (henceforth max-speed) of a cell could be several times higher than its average speed (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by speed profile analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: Max-speeds varied across cells in a smooth distribution from 183 μm/hr to 0 μm/hr for controls and from 134 μm/hr to 0 μm/hr for Dab1-/- cells.
source: Furthermore, ranking all control and all Dab1-/- cells by their max-speeds revealed great diversity as the max-speeds varied across cells in a smooth distribution from 183 μm/hr to 0 μm/hr for controls and from 134 μm/hr to 0 μm/hr for Dab1-/- cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: This is supported by analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The effect of Reelin on the speed of migrating neurons varies depending on the brain region and type of neuron analyzed.
source: The role of Reelin signaling has been studied extensively in the cortex and hippocampus. However, only few studies have examined Reelin function in regulating the speed of migrating neurons. These studies have shown that the effect of Reelin varies depending on the brain region and type of neuron analyzed (Simó et al., 2010; Britto et al., 2014; Britto et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Inhibiting Reelin in ex vivo slices results in a decrease in average speed of SN-mDA neurons over long periods of imaging.
source: We have previously demonstrated that inhibiting Reelin in ex vivo slices results in a decrease in average speed of SN-mDA neurons over long periods of imaging (Bodea et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work from the authors' laboratory.

claim: There was no significant difference in the overall distribution of average speeds of the SN-mDA population in Dab1-/- slices compared to control slices.
source: In our current analysis we found no significant difference in the overall distribution of average speeds of the SN-mDA population in Dab1-/- slices compared to control slices (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: Overall distribution of max-speeds was significantly shifted towards lower speeds in the absence of Reelin signaling.
source: However, overall distribution of max-speeds was significantly shifted towards lower speeds in the absence of Reelin signaling (control: 25thpercentile = 12.4 μm/hr, median = 23.6 μm/hr, 75thpercentile = 48.1 μm/hr, maximum = 183 μm/hr; Dab1-/-: 25thpercentile = 10.1 μm/hr, median = 15 μm/hr, 75thpercentile = 29.8 μm/hr, maximum = 133.7 μm/hr; Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: Total displacement (3D) of mDA neurons is significantly higher in moderate compared to slow mDA neurons in both control and Dab1-/- brains.
source: Total displacement (3D) of mDA neurons is significantly higher in moderate compared to slow mDA neurons, and higher in fast mDA neurons compared to moderate neurons in both control (C) and Dab1-/- (D) brains (****p<0.0001, **p<0.01, Kruskal-Wallis test; n = 680 control; n = 639 Dab1-/- cells, three slices/genotype).
evidence: This is supported by quantification and statistical analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: Total displacement (3D) of mDA neurons is higher in fast mDA neurons compared to moderate neurons in both control and Dab1-/- brains.
source: Total displacement (3D) of mDA neurons is significantly higher in moderate compared to slow mDA neurons, and higher in fast mDA neurons compared to moderate neurons in both control (C) and Dab1-/- (D) brains (****p<0.0001, **p<0.01, Kruskal-Wallis test; n = 680 control; n = 639 Dab1-/- cells, three slices/genotype).
evidence: This is supported by quantification and statistical analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: Directionality in control and Dab1-/- slices is the least in slow mDA neurons, higher in moderate mDA neurons and the highest in fast mDA neurons.
source: Directionality (defined as ratio of total displacement to path length) in control and Dab1-/- slices is the least in slow mDA neurons, higher in moderate mDA neurons and the highest in fast mDA neurons (*p<0.05, **p<0.01, ****p<0.0001, Kruskal-Wallis test; n = 680 control; n = 639 Dab1-/- cells, three slices/genotype).
evidence: This is supported by quantification and statistical analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: In control slices, 'fast', 'moderate' and 'slow' cells spent a predominant fraction of time at rest.
source: In control slices, 'fast', 'moderate' and 'slow' cells spent a predominant fraction of time at rest (62.6 ± 20%; 68.5 ± 18.2%, 85.7 ± 11.1%, respectively) and were frequently in a slow migratory phase (26.8 ± 17.4%, 25.1 ± 16.3%, 14.2 ± 11.1%, respectively).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of time spent in different migratory phases.

claim: 'Fast' and 'moderate' cells achieved the moderate migratory phase in only a few frames.
source: 'Fast' and 'moderate' cells achieved the moderate migratory phase in only a few frames (5.5 ± 5.5% and 6.3 ± 3.9, respectively), and the fast migratory phase (only in 'fast' cells) was equally infrequent (5.5 ± 2.2%) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The amount of time SN-mDA neurons of the same max-speed group spent in the resting phase or in the respective migratory phases was comparable between individual cells in control and Dab1-/- slices.
source: The amount of time SN-mDA neurons of the same max-speed group spent in the resting phase or in the respective migratory phases was comparable between individual cells in control and Dab1-/- slices (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D–F).
evidence: This is supported by analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: SN-mDA migration has two distinct modes: a frequent slow migration phase seen in all migrating SN-mDA neurons and an infrequent moderate-to-fast phase occurring in a subset of SN-mDA neurons.
source: In summary, these results demonstrate that SN-mDA migration has two distinct modes: a frequent slow migration phase seen in all migrating SN-mDA neurons and an infrequent moderate-to-fast phase occurring in a subset of SN-mDA neurons.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the speed analysis.

claim: Reelin signaling increases the proportion of migratory mDA neurons and the likelihood of moderate-to-fast movements in migrating mDA neurons.
source: Reelin signaling increases the proportion of migratory mDA neurons and the likelihood of moderate-to-fast movements in migrating mDA neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the comparison of control and Dab1-/- neurons.

claim: Directionality as well as total displacement generally increased with increasing max-speeds in SN-mDA populations from both control and Dab1-/- slices.
source: We found that directionality as well as total displacement generally increased with increasing max-speeds in SN-mDA populations from both control and Dab1-/- slices (Figure 5C–F; Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by analysis shown in Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The infrequent moderate-to-fast movements in SN-mDA neurons result in major contributions to the directed migration of these cells.
source: These data indicate that the infrequent moderate-to-fast movements in SN-mDA neurons result in major contributions to the directed migration of these cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the relationship between speed and directionality.

claim: Reelin supports directed migration of mDA neurons on a population level.
source: Since Reelin signaling increases the fraction of SN-mDA neurons that are able to undergo moderate-to-fast movements, Reelin supports directed migration of mDA neurons on a population level.
evidence: This is an inference based on the effect of Reelin on the proportion of fast-migrating cells.

claim: SN-mDA neurons from control slices displayed an anisotropy towards lateral migratory directions (mean 92.5°, σang 68.4).
source: We found that SN-mDA neurons from control slices displayed an anisotropy towards lateral migratory directions (mean 92.5°, σang 68.4) while Dab1-/- SN-mDA neurons showed a significantly reduced preference for lateral migration (mean 27.5°, σang 70.4) (Figure 6B–D; see materials and methods for analysis of circular variables).
evidence: This is supported by trajectory analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: Dab1-/- SN-mDA neurons showed a significantly reduced preference for lateral migration (mean 27.5°, σang 70.4).
source: We found that SN-mDA neurons from control slices displayed an anisotropy towards lateral migratory directions (mean 92.5°, σang 68.4) while Dab1-/- SN-mDA neurons showed a significantly reduced preference for lateral migration (mean 27.5°, σang 70.4) (Figure 6B–D; see materials and methods for analysis of circular variables).
evidence: This is supported by trajectory analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: Trajectories of all three SN-mDA groups ('fast', 'moderate', 'slow') were anisotropic in controls, favoring migration towards lateral directions.
source: We found that trajectories of all three SN-mDA groups were anisotropic in controls, favoring migration towards lateral directions, but this anisotropy was greater in 'fast' and 'moderate' cells than in 'slow' cells (Figure 7A,D,G).
evidence: This is supported by trajectory analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: The anisotropy towards lateral directions was greater in 'fast' and 'moderate' cells than in 'slow' cells in controls.
source: We found that trajectories of all three SN-mDA groups were anisotropic in controls, favoring migration towards lateral directions, but this anisotropy was greater in 'fast' and 'moderate' cells than in 'slow' cells (Figure 7A,D,G).
evidence: This is supported by trajectory analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: Individual moderate-to-fast phases were more anisotropic than slow phases.
source: Resolving this further into individual slow, moderate and fast migratory phases in the migratory mDA population, we also found that individual moderate-to-fast phases were more anisotropic than slow phases (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,C,E).
evidence: This is supported by analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: In the absence of Reelin signaling, the trajectory profiles of 'slow' neurons were significantly altered with a complete loss of anisotropy towards lateral directions (mean −12.3°, σang 69.7°).
source: In the absence of Reelin signaling, the trajectory profiles of 'slow' neurons were significantly altered with a complete loss of anisotropy towards lateral directions (mean −12.3°, σang 69.7°) (Figure 7A–C).
evidence: This is supported by trajectory analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: 'Fast' and 'moderate' neurons still navigated to more lateral regions in Dab1-/- slices and their trajectory angle distributions were nearly identical to control neurons.
source: In contrast, 'fast' and 'moderate' neurons still navigated to more lateral regions in Dab1-/- slices and their trajectory angle distributions were nearly identical to control neurons (Dab1-/- 'fast' neurons: mean 81°, σang 57.9°; 'moderate' neurons: mean 69.4°, σang 58.7°) (Figure 7D–I).
evidence: This is supported by trajectory analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: Slow phases are weakly laterally-directed in controls, but in the absence of Reelin signaling individual slow migratory movements lose their slight lateral preference.
source: This finding also applies to slow, moderate and fast phases: slow phases are weakly laterally-directed in controls, but in the absence of Reelin signaling individual slow migratory movements lose their slight lateral preference (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B,D,F and data not shown).
evidence: This is supported by analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Reelin signaling promotes lateral migration of SN-mDA neurons by increasing the fraction of SN-mDA neurons undergoing moderate-to-fast movements that are strongly biased for tangential movements and by promoting lateral anisotropy of slowly migrating neurons.
source: These results show that Reelin signaling promotes lateral migration of SN-mDA neurons by increasing the fraction of SN-mDA neurons undergoing moderate-to-fast movements that are strongly biased for tangential movements and by promoting lateral anisotropy of slowly migrating neurons.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the trajectory analysis.

claim: Some mDA cells had a stable, unbranched leading process (LP), and did not change their morphology.
source: Some cells had a stable, unbranched leading process (LP), and did not change their morphology, while other cells displayed dynamic LPs, that extended, retracted and branched frequently over time (Figure 8A–D; Figure 8—figure supplement 1; Video 2).
evidence: This is supported by morphological analysis shown in Figure 8 and supplementary figures.

claim: Other mDA cells displayed dynamic LPs, that extended, retracted and branched frequently over time.
source: Some cells had a stable, unbranched leading process (LP), and did not change their morphology, while other cells displayed dynamic LPs, that extended, retracted and branched frequently over time (Figure 8A–D; Figure 8—figure supplement 1; Video 2).
evidence: This is supported by morphological analysis shown in Figure 8 and supplementary figures.

claim: In both control and Dab1-/- SN-mDA neurons, fast and moderate migratory phases were almost exclusively associated with bipolar morphology.
source: Bipolarity was predominant in all phases of migration, but in both control and Dab1-/- SN-mDA neurons, fast and moderate migratory phases were almost exclusively associated with bipolar morphology.
evidence: This is supported by morphological analysis shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2.

claim: About a third of slow migratory phases were associated with multipolar morphology in both control and Dab1-/- SN-mDA neurons.
source: In contrast, about a third of slow migratory phases were associated with multipolar morphology (Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by morphological analysis shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2.

claim: While slow migratory phases can occur in either bipolar or multipolar morphology, fast and moderate migration events are predominantly associated with bipolar morphology.
source: Hence, while slow migratory phases can occur in either bipolar or multipolar morphology, fast and moderate migration events are predominantly associated with bipolar morphology.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the morphological analysis.

claim: In controls, transitionary cells made up about 40% of the total population.
source: In controls, transitionary cells made up about 40% of the total population.
evidence: This is supported by morphological analysis.

claim: The proportion of transitionary cells was significantly increased in the Dab1-/- population, while the population of bipolar neurons was decreased.
source: The proportion of transitionary cells was significantly increased in the Dab1-/- population, while the population of bipolar neurons was decreased (Figure 8E, Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by morphological analysis shown in Figure 8 and Table 1.

claim: Within the transitionary population, there was no difference in the frequency of transitions between bipolar and multipolar morphologies for each neuron in Dab1-/- compared to control slices.
source: Within the transitionary population, we found however no difference in the frequency of transitions between bipolar and multipolar morphologies for each neuron (defined as number of morphology transitions per hour) in Dab1-/- compared to control slices (Figure 8F).
evidence: This is supported by morphological analysis shown in Figure 8.

claim: Branch transition events were significantly more frequent in Dab1-/- SN-mDA transitionary neurons.
source: We found that these branch transition events were significantly more frequent in Dab1-/- SN-mDA transitionary neurons (Figure 8H), since Dab1-/- neurons displayed short, transient protrusions that appeared on the soma and LP for only a few time frames before disappearing (Figure 8—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by morphological analysis shown in Figure 8.

claim: Dab1-/- neurons displayed short, transient protrusions that appeared on the soma and LP for only a few time frames before disappearing.
source: We found that these branch transition events were significantly more frequent in Dab1-/- SN-mDA transitionary neurons (Figure 8H), since Dab1-/- neurons displayed short, transient protrusions that appeared on the soma and LP for only a few time frames before disappearing (Figure 8—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by morphological analysis shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 3.

claim: In all control and Dab1-/- mDA neurons, the LP remained stable and visible during the duration of imaging.
source: In all control and Dab1-/- mDA neurons, the LP remained stable and visible during the duration of imaging.
evidence: This is based on manual tracing of neurons.

claim: mDA neurons in Dab1-/- slices displayed a broader distribution of LP length with very long and very short LPs.
source: We then compared the length of the LP (plus cell body) in control and Dab1-/- mDA neurons and found that mDA neurons in Dab1-/- slices displayed a broader distribution of LP length with very long and very short LPs (Figure 8—figure supplement 4G).
evidence: This is supported by morphological analysis shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 4.

claim: In the absence of Reelin signaling, SN-mDA neurons display aberrant changes in morphology characterized by an increased proportion of transitionary neurons, an increase in unstable processes on the cell soma and LP and a greater variation in LP length.
source: Hence, in the absence of Reelin signaling, SN-mDA neurons display aberrant changes in morphology characterized by an increased proportion of transitionary neurons, an increase in unstable processes on the cell soma and LP and a greater variation in LP length.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the morphological analysis.

claim: Relative phosphorylation levels of LIMK1 are not significantly altered in Dab1-/- ventral midbrains.
source: Relative phosphorylation levels of LIMK1 are not significantly altered in Dab1-/- ventral midbrains. p-value=0.5682, Student's t-test (n = 5 brains/genotype).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 9.

claim: Relative phosphorylation levels of Cofilin1 are not significantly changed in Dab1-/- ventral midbrains.
source: Relative phosphorylation levels of Cofilin1 are not significantly changed in Dab1-/- ventral midbrains. p-value=0.854, Student's t-test (n = 5 brains/genotype).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 9.

claim: The regulation of LIMK1/Cofilin1 activity is unlikely to be the key event in controlling cytoskeletal stability in migrating mDA neurons downstream of Reelin signaling.
source: Hence, we conclude that the regulation of LIMK1/Cofilin1 activity is unlikely to be the key event in controlling cytoskeletal stability in migrating mDA neurons downstream of Reelin signaling.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the immunoblotting results.

claim: Reelin signaling controls somal translocation of radially migrating cortical neurons by modulating cell adhesion properties through regulation of CDH2 via the Crk/C3G/Rap1 pathway.
source: Reelin signaling controls somal translocation of radially migrating cortical neurons by modulating cell adhesion properties through regulation of CDH2 via the Crk/C3G/Rap1 pathway (Jossin and Cooper, 2011; Gärtner et al., 2012; Gil-Sanz et al., 2013; Cooper, 2014; Matsunaga et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Relative protein levels of CDH2 were similar in tissue lysates from control and Dab1-/- E14.5 ventral midbrain.
source: Relative protein levels of CDH2 were similar in tissue lysates from control and Dab1-/- E14.5 ventral midbrain (Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: In the cortex, Reelin positively regulates microtubule dynamics in cortical neurons during development.
source: In the cortex, Reelin positively regulates microtubule dynamics in cortical neurons during development (Meseke et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: No obvious change was detected in the distribution or expression level of α-tubulin, acetylated α-tubulin and EB3 in the ventral midbrain of Dab1-/- embryos.
source: In contrast to what has been reported in the cortex, we could however not detect an obvious change in the distribution or expression level of these tubulin markers in the ventral midbrain of Dab1-/-embryos (Figure 9—figure supplement 2), indicating that the loss of Dab1 has likely no major effect on the microtubule cytoskeleton.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 2.

claim: The loss of Dab1 has likely no major effect on the microtubule cytoskeleton in the ventral midbrain.
source: In contrast to what has been reported in the cortex, we could however not detect an obvious change in the distribution or expression level of these tubulin markers in the ventral midbrain of Dab1-/-embryos (Figure 9—figure supplement 2), indicating that the loss of Dab1 has likely no major effect on the microtubule cytoskeleton.
evidence: This is an inference based on the immunostaining results.

claim: Reelin is directly required for the stabilization of the LP and for the orientation of radially-migrating cortical projection neurons.
source: Studies in cortex have shown that while Reelin is directly required for the stabilization of the LP and for the orientation of radially-migrating cortical projection neurons (Franco et al., 2011), Reelin also indirectly affects migration through regulating radial glia cell process extension, morphology and maturation (Hartfuss et al., 2003; Keilani and Sugaya, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Reelin indirectly affects migration in the cortex through regulating radial glia cell process extension, morphology and maturation.
source: Studies in cortex have shown that while Reelin is directly required for the stabilization of the LP and for the orientation of radially-migrating cortical projection neurons (Franco et al., 2011), Reelin also indirectly affects migration through regulating radial glia cell process extension, morphology and maturation (Hartfuss et al., 2003; Keilani and Sugaya, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Tangentially migrating cortical interneurons are only indirectly affected by Reelin signaling.
source: Tangentially migrating cortical interneurons are only indirectly affected by Reelin signaling: the improper cortical layering caused by defective radial migration in absence of Reelin signaling ultimately results in mispositioning of interneurons (Yabut et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Reelin acts as a detachment signal that regulates the switch from tangential chain migration to radial migration in interneuron precursors migrating to the olfactory bulb.
source: Reelin also plays a role in interneuron precursors that undergo tangential chain migration to the olfactory bulb. However, it does not modulate tangential migration directly but rather acts as a detachment signal that regulates the switch form tangential chain migration to radial migration (Hack et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: In sympathetic preganglionic neurons in the spinal cord, Reelin stabilizes LPs via the phosphorylation of Cofilin during tangential migration thereby preventing aberrant migration.
source: Evidence for a direct function of Reelin signaling in tangential neuronal migration comes from sympathetic preganglionic neurons in the spinal cord. In these neurons, Reelin has been shown to stabilize LPs via the phosphorylation of during tangential migration thereby preventing aberrant migration (Phelps et al., 2002; Krüger et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The similarity in mediolateral distribution of SN-mDA neurons in Dab1-/- and in Dab1 CKO implies that Reelin signaling has a direct effect on migrating SN-mDA neurons.
source: The similarity in mediolateral distribution of SN-mDA neurons in Dab1-/- and in Dab1 CKO implies that Reelin signaling has a direct effect on migrating SN-mDA neurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of phenotypes.

claim: The inactivation of Dab1 in mDA neurons and the disorganization of the SN and VTA did not obviously alter the density of projections to the striatum.
source: Interestingly, the inactivation of Dab1 in mDA neurons and the disorganization of the SN and VTA did not obviously alter the density of projections to the striatum.
evidence: This is based on analysis of axonal projections.

claim: The axons of mislocalized mDA neurons may still find their way and correct position in the medial forebrain bundle and then rely on intrinsic markers (cell adhesion molecules) to navigate to their particular projection target.
source: This indicates that the axons of mislocalized mDA neurons may still find their way and correct position in the medial forebrain bundle and then rely on intrinsic markers (cell adhesion molecules) to navigate to their particular projection target (Brignani and Pasterkamp, 2017).
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that projections are not obviously altered, supported by citation.

claim: In the ventral midbrain, Reelin mRNA is restricted to the cells of the red nucleus at E13.5 and E14.5.
source: In the ventral midbrain, Reelin mRNA is restricted to the cells of the red nucleus at E13.5 and E14.5 (Bodea et al., 2014; Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2 and citation to previous work.

claim: Reelin protein is distributed more broadly at E13.5 and E14.5 than Reelin mRNA.
source: Using immunostaining, we show that Reelin protein is distributed more broadly at these stages.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Strong Reelin labeling is seen in regions lateral to the migrating SN-mDA at E13.5 and E14.5.
source: Strong labeling is seen in regions lateral to the migrating SN-mDA, while weaker staining is observed in the area where SN-mDA neurons are localized.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Weaker Reelin staining is observed in the area where SN-mDA neurons are localized at E13.5 and E14.5.
source: Strong labeling is seen in regions lateral to the migrating SN-mDA, while weaker staining is observed in the area where SN-mDA neurons are localized.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Whether the red nucleus is the only source for Reelin in the ventral midbrain or whether there are additional sources remains to be investigated.
source: Whether the red nucleus is the only source for Reelin in the ventral midbrain or whether there are additional sources remains to be investigated.
evidence: This is a statement about a gap in knowledge.

claim: Mouse mutants in which the RN is only partially formed do not show any obvious displacement of SN-mDA neurons (at least not up to E18.5).
source: Mouse mutants in which the RN is only partially formed do not show any obvious displacement of SN-mDA neurons (at least not up to E18.5), suggesting that other Reelin sources could be important for mDA migration (Prakash et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Reelin mRNA is expressed in the hypothalamus and ventral thalamus anterior to the SN.
source: Reelin mRNA is expressed anterior to the SN, in the hypothalamus and ventral thalamus (Alcántara et al., 1998; Allen Institute, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research and database.

claim: It has been proposed that Reelin is transported from the striatum to the SN via axons in the striatonigral pathway.
source: Moreover, it has been proposed that Reelin is transported from the striatum to the SN via axons in the striatonigral pathway (Nishikawa et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Reelin is expressed in the early differentiating cells in the striatum.
source: Indeed, Reelin is expressed in the early differentiating cells in the striatum, but the striatonigral pathway is only established (E17 in rat) after the critical time period for SN-mDA migration (Fishell and van der Kooy, 1987; Alcántara et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The striatonigral pathway is only established (E17 in rat) after the critical time period for SN-mDA migration.
source: Indeed, Reelin is expressed in the early differentiating cells in the striatum, but the striatonigral pathway is only established (E17 in rat) after the critical time period for SN-mDA migration (Fishell and van der Kooy, 1987; Alcántara et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Irrespective of their max-speed, mDA neurons spent a majority of their time at rest.
source: The visualization and tracking of a large population of migrating mDA neurons, and the subsequent categorization of the instantaneous soma speed of individual mDA neurons into slow, moderate and fast phases revealed that irrespective of their max-speed, mDA neurons spent a majority of their time at rest.
evidence: This is based on analysis of time spent in different migratory phases.

claim: During their migratory phase, mDA neurons move mostly at slow speed.
source: During their migratory phase, mDA neurons move mostly at slow speed.
evidence: This is based on analysis of time spent in different migratory phases.

claim: Moderate-to-fast laterally-directed migration spurts that result in large displacements are infrequent and occur in only a subset of labeled mDA neurons during the time-window of imaging.
source: Moderate-to-fast laterally-directed migration spurts that result in large displacements are infrequent and occur in only a subset of labeled mDA neurons during the time-window of imaging.
evidence: This is based on analysis of migration speeds and frequencies.

claim: A similar pattern of migration with variable instantaneous speeds and periods of rest has been reported for newly generated granule cells in the dentate gyrus and for cortical projection neurons.
source: A similar pattern of migration with variable instantaneous speeds and periods of rest has also been reported for newly generated granule cells in the dentate gyrus and for cortical projection neurons (Simó et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.
